title: Final exam: sets, maps & priority queues
overview: Shammunul's solutions to the course final exam. Each question is a small data-handling task that becomes easy once you pick the right STL container: a `set` to sort and remove duplicates, a priority queue with a custom comparator to order pairs or students, a `map` to count words, and a min-heap to answer 'current minimum' queries. Revise these to practise choosing a container quickly.

concepts.term: Pick the container from the question
concepts.explain: 'Sorted and unique' means `set`. 'How many times' means `map`. 'Current min/max while items come and go' means `priority_queue`.
Compare the main key first; only when it ties, compare the second key. In a priority queue, return true when the left item should come out later.
concepts.snippet: if(l.name != r.name) return l.name > r.name; return l.val < r.val;

concepts.term: Reading a number, then whole lines
concepts.explain: After `cin >> T`, the newline is still waiting in the input. `cin.ignore()` throws it away so the next `getline` reads the real sentence.

concepts.term: First word to reach the maximum
concepts.explain: Update the answer only when a count becomes **strictly** greater than the best so far. A later word that only ties does not replace it.
concepts.snippet: if(freq[w] > best){ best = freq[w]; ans = w; }

concepts.explain: Before `top()` or `pop()`, check `empty()` and print `Empty` instead. After a pop, check again before printing the new top.

concepts.term: map vs. vector of pairs for counting
concepts.explain: A `map` finds a word in O(log n). Searching a vector of pairs is O(n) per word, which can be too slow for long inputs.

files.title: Q1: Sorted (sort and remove duplicates)
files.what: For each test case, puts the numbers into a `set` and prints them, which gives sorted order with duplicates removed.
steps: Read `T`, the number of test cases.
For each case, create a fresh `set<int> A` and insert the `N` numbers.
Walk the set from `begin()` to `end()` and print each value, then a newline.
files.complexity: Time O(N log N) per case · Space O(N)
files.input_note: T, then for each case N and a line of N numbers.
files.output_note: The runner shows a compile error, so no output appears. Once fixed, it would print `0 3 5 6 9 10` and `3 7`.
files.watch_out: Does not compile: the file includes `<iostream>` and `<set>` but never writes `using namespace std;`, so `cin`, `cout` and `set` are unknown. Fix: add `using namespace std;` after the includes.

check.q: Why is a new `set` created inside the loop instead of once outside it?
check.a: So each test case starts empty; otherwise numbers from earlier cases would be printed too.

files.title: Q2: Pairs (sort by name, then value descending)
files.what: Puts (name, value) pairs into a priority queue whose comparator gives names in ascending order and, for equal names, values in descending order.
steps: `Pair` holds a `name` and a `val`.
In `cmp`, `l.name > r.name` returns true, so later names sink and the alphabetically smallest name comes out first.
For equal names, `l.val < r.val` returns true, so the larger value comes out first.
Push all N pairs, then print `top()` and `pop()` until empty.
files.complexity: Time O(N log N) · Space O(N)
files.input_note: N, then N lines of `name value`.
files.watch_out: `main` has no `return 0;`. That is allowed in C++ (main returns 0 by default), but add it for consistency.

check.q: With `sakib 5`, `sakib 6`, `sakib 4`, in what order are they printed?
check.a: `sakib 6`, `sakib 5`, `sakib 4`, because equal names are ordered by value, largest first.

files.title: Pairs (copy of Q2)
files.what: The same solution as Q2 with `return 0;` added at the end. Here it is tried with the input that has repeated names.
steps: Same `Pair` class and `cmp` comparator as Q2.
The repeated name `sakib` shows the tie-break: bigger value first.
files.complexity: Time O(N log N) · Space O(N)
files.input:
6
sakib 5
rakib 3
tasfia 2
sakib 6
afia 1
sakib 4
files.input_note: N, then N lines of `name value`.
files.output_note: `afia 1`, `rakib 3`, then the three `sakib` lines as 6, 5, 4, then `tasfia 2`.

check.q: Which line of `cmp` decides the order of the three `sakib` pairs?

files.title: Q3: Count Me (vector of pairs)
files.what: Finds the most frequent word in each sentence by keeping (word, count) pairs in a vector and searching it for every word.
steps: `cin.ignore()` after reading `T` removes the leftover newline so `getline` reads the sentence.
For each word, a loop searches `word_freq`; if found, its count goes up, and the answer changes only when the count beats `count_max`.
A new word is pushed with count 1 without touching the answer.
After the sentence, a final loop picks the first word whose count beats `count_max`. This only matters when every word appears once (`count_max` is still 0), and then it picks the first word.
Print the word and its count.
files.complexity: Time O(w^2) per sentence for w words · Space O(w)
files.input:
2
ratul piyush fohad shuvo rafi piyush fohad ratul
a b c
files.input_note: T, then T sentences, one per line.
files.output_note: `piyush 2`: piyush, fohad and ratul all reach 2, but piyush gets there first. `a 1`: all words appear once, so the final loop picks the first one.
files.watch_out: The search through the vector is linear for every word, so long sentences get slow. The `map` version fixes this.

check.q: In the first sentence, why is the answer not `ratul`, even though it appears first?
check.a: The rule is the first word to **reach** the top count; ratul's second copy is the last word, after piyush has already reached 2.

files.title: Q3: Count Me (map)
files.what: The same task with a `map<string,int>`: count each word and update the answer the moment a count beats the best so far.
steps: Read `T`, then `cin.ignore()`, then each sentence with `getline`.
`word_freq[word] = word_freq[word] + 1` counts the word (a new word starts at 0).
If the new count is greater than `count_max`, save this word as `result`.
Because the check is strict (`>`), a word that only ties never replaces the earlier one.
Print `result` and `count_max`.
files.complexity: Time O(w log w) per sentence · Space O(w)
files.input:
2
ratul piyush fohad shuvo rafi piyush fohad ratul
jony jony yes papa eating sugar no papa telling lies no papa
files.input_note: T, then T sentences, one per line.
files.output_note: `piyush 2` for the first sentence and `papa 3` for the second (jony and no reach 2, but papa is the only word to reach 3).
files.watch_out: Without `cin.ignore()`, the first `getline` would read an empty line and print a blank answer.

check.q: Why does this version not need the final loop that the vector version has?
check.a: Every word, even a first appearance, is checked against `count_max` right after counting, so a count of 1 already sets the answer.

files.title: Q4: Give Current Min
files.what: Keeps the numbers in a min-heap and answers three commands: insert and show the min, show the min, delete the min and show the new min.
steps: Push the first N numbers into `priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq`.
Command `0 X`: push X, then print `pq.top()` (never empty here).
Command `1`: print `Empty` if the heap is empty, otherwise the top.
Command `2`: if empty, print `Empty`; otherwise pop, then print the new top or `Empty` if nothing is left.
files.complexity: Each command O(log n) · Space O(N + Q)
files.input_note: N, the N numbers, Q, then Q commands.
files.output_note: `-20` (min), `-10` (after deleting -20), `-30` (just inserted), then `-10`, `-5`, `10` as each minimum is deleted.

check.q: Heap holds only 7. Command `2` arrives. What is printed?
check.a: `Empty`, because 7 is removed and nothing is left to show.

files.title: Q5: Give Current Max (students)
files.what: The same three commands as Q4, but for students in a max-heap ordered by marks (highest first) and then by roll (smallest first).
steps: `cmp` returns true when `l.marks < r.marks`, so the highest marks rise to the top.
On equal marks, `l.roll > r.roll` returns true, so the smaller roll is on top.
Command `0 name roll marks`: push the student and print the top student.
Command `1`: print the top student or `Empty`.
Command `2`: pop (if possible), then print the new top or `Empty`.
files.complexity: Each command O(log n) · Space O(N + Q)
files.input_note: N, N student lines, Q, then Q commands.
files.output_note: `ali 25 100` (top), `jobbar 24 99` (ali removed), `kabir 15 99` (ties jobbar on 99 but has the smaller roll), `asif 10 99` (smaller roll still), then `kabir 15 99` and `jobbar 24 99` as the tops are removed.
files.watch_out: The three command checks use separate `if`s instead of `else if`. It still works because `x` has only one value, but `else if` shows the intent better.

check.q: Two students both have 80 marks, rolls 7 and 3. Who is printed as the max?
check.a: The one with roll 3, because on equal marks the smaller roll wins.

recap: Sorted and unique → `set`; counting → `map`; changing min/max → `priority_queue`.
Multi-key comparator: compare the main key, and use the second key only on a tie.
'First to reach the max' means updating only on a strictly greater count.
Check `empty()` before every `top()` and `pop()`, and again after popping.
Don't forget `using namespace std;` when you don't use `bits/stdc++.h`.

check_yourself.q: Q4 asks for the current **maximum** instead. What is the smallest change to the code?
check_yourself.a: Use `priority_queue<int>` (the default max-heap) instead of the `greater<int>` version.

check_yourself.q: In the Pairs comparator, what happens if you change `l.name > r.name` to `l.name < r.name`?
check_yourself.a: Names come out in reverse alphabetical order.

check_yourself.q: In the sentence `x y y x`, which word does Count Me print, and why?
check_yourself.a: `y 2`, because y reaches 2 at the third word, before x reaches 2 at the fourth.

check_yourself.q: Why is a sorted `vector` with `unique` also a valid answer to Q1, and why is `set` simpler?
check_yourself.a: Sorting then `unique` + `erase` removes adjacent duplicates; a `set` does both jobs automatically as you insert.

body: This is the final exam of the course, and the hard part is not writing the code. It is reading a question and deciding, inside a minute, which container answers it. The whole course points at that one decision, so here is the map:
intro.trace:
the question asks for        reach for
---------------------------  ------------------
sorted, no duplicates        set
how many times, or which     map
  word or value wins
the smallest or biggest one  priority_queue
  right now, while items
  keep arriving and leaving
the answer for a position,   prefix sums
  from sums of the rest
first in first out / last    queue / stack
  in first out
search by comparing, and     BST
  in-order comes out sorted

body: The pattern that comes up most is counting with a `map` and then picking the best count, so trace it once before the exam. Read the words with `getline` and a `stringstream`, tick a box per word, and keep track of the best as you go.

The trap is the tie. If the question wants the **first** word to reach the highest count, update the answer only when the new count is strictly greater than the best so far. Using `>=` would let a later word steal the place on a tie:
intro.trace:
sentence: bat cat bat cat dog

word   its count   best so far
bat        1        bat 1
cat        1        bat 1
bat        2        bat 2
cat        2        bat 2   (tie: no change)
dog        1        bat 2

answer: bat 2

body: The second pattern is a pile that changes while you are being asked about it. Keep the numbers in a min-heap and the current smallest is always `top()`, whatever has been added or removed since. Nothing is re-sorted, and each command costs O(log n):
intro.trace:
start with 7 3 9      min-heap top = 3
insert 5           -> top 3
ask for the min    -> 3
delete the min     -> 5 is now on top
delete the min     -> 7 is now on top
delete the min     -> 9 is now on top
delete the min     -> nothing left: Empty

body: Watch that last line. A delete question asks for the minimum **after** the deletion, so the heap can be empty by the time you print. Check `empty()` before every `top()` and `pop()`, and check again after popping, or the program prints rubbish on the last query.

Three more things that cost marks rather than ideas. After `cin >> T` the newline is still sitting in the input, so `cin.ignore()` must come before the first `getline`. In a priority queue comparator with two keys, compare the main key and only fall through to the second when the first ties, and remember that returning true means the left item comes out **later**. And counting words in a vector of pairs works, but each word is an O(n) search through it, so a long input runs out of time where a `map` at O(log n) does not.
The solutions below are Shammunul's answers to the five questions. Read each problem first and choose your container before looking, then compare; that is the part the exam actually tests.
